newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX Dec natgas bolts to new high before expiry.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX Dec natgas bolts to new high before expiry.

text.p: After a brief retreat into negative territory midday Thursday, NYMEX December Henry Hub natural gas futures capped a six-day rally with a last minute run before expiration to another all-time high.

While the midday pullback was expected by chartists who felt some longs were bound to exit before the spot contract went off the board, most saw only limited downside with an Arctic air mass slated to blanket the nation next week.
"I'm not going to try to predict prices, but I don't see a major meltdown based on the fundamentals," said Smith Barney analyst John Saucer in Houston.
December expired 27.4 cents higher Thursday at $3.901 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), after earlier setting an all-time intraday high of $4.050.
January, which moves into the spot position Friday, settled up four cents at $3.304 after climbing earlier to a new benchmark of $3.450.

Traders said revised forecasts showing even more cold air spilling across the country than first predicted and strong December cash differentials helped spook the shorts out of the market and drive the spot contract up as high as 53 percent in the last six sessions.
The contract, using settlement instead of intraday prices, expired 47 percent higher over the same six sessions.
"The fact that December basis stayed real tight all week caused the shorts to capitulate. Weak shorts had to get out at any price," said one East Coast trader.
And most expected January to resume the climb, with more cold ahead and futures still at a serious discount to cash.
Physical gas for December delivery at Henry Hub traded late Thursday in the mid-$3.80s, about 55 cents over the January settlement.
"Short-term, January could stay firm with the weather. It's trading at such a large discount to December you could see a rally to get the spread back in line," said a trader.
Traders also said extreme cold in western Canada was draining potential exports to the U.S., further tightening supply.

"The Rockies and Midcontinent cannot service peak day load (in the U.S.) without Canadian gas. We've seen a flip flop in basis for the first time," said one Houston-based player, referring to some price quotes in west Texas above the Gulf Coast for the first time.
While the first sign of more seasonal weather could trigger a selloff, traders said concerns about storage, at least early in the season, should help limit any decline.

American Gas Association data Wednesday showed U.S. gas stocks fell last week by 86 billion cubic feet (bcf) to 82 percent of capacity, at the high end of expectations. Overall inventories were still 181 bcf, or six percent, below year-ago, with Producing Region storage at just 69 percent full, well-below last year.
"We're going to have a pretty big (stock) drawdown in November and people will be even more inclined to husband storage next month," said Smith Barney's Saucer.
